%%%%%% -- PAPER CONTENT STARTS-- %%%%%%%%

\begin{abstract}

Indirect memory access (IMA) patterns---where one load's address
depends on the value returned by a prior load, as in
$A[B[i]]$---dominate L1 cache misses in graph analytics and sparse
workloads on GPUs, contributing 61--93\% of all L1 data misses
across six representative graph algorithms. The serial dependency
between index and data loads inflates per-access latency to
$\approx{}786$~cycles, which would require roughly $3{\times}$ the
64-warp ceiling of an A100 SM to hide through warp parallelism
alone---making prefetching the natural remedy.

Yet no existing prefetcher handles this pattern on modern GPUs.
Fifteen years of GPU prefetching has targeted stride-based
accesses and explicitly skips data-dependent loads, while CPU IMA
prefetchers assume a single sequential instruction stream whose
per-core state would cost 36.5--57.6~KB per SM if replicated
across 64 warps.

We observe that the GPU's SASS ISA already exposes every
parameter needed for IMA prefetching: NVIDIA's \texttt{IMAD.WIDE}
instruction encodes the data array's base pointer, element scale,
and index source register directly as operands, so a single
instruction-level observation at the issue stage yields the full
prefetch descriptor with zero inference. Building on this, we
propose \textbf{GRASP}, which detects
\texttt{LDG}$\to$\texttt{IMAD.WIDE}$\to$\texttt{LDG} dependency
chains at issue, runs a two-step index-then-data prefetch
pipeline, and merges compiler-induced PC proliferation onto
shared per-SM tables via \emph{(base, scale)} keys.

Evaluated on 28~workloads spanning six graph algorithms and five
datasets with an A100 configuration in Accel-Sim, GRASP achieves
a geometric-mean speedup of \textbf{1.18$\times$} (up to
\textbf{2.22$\times$})---ahead of Snake ($1.04\times$), CAPS
($1.00\times$), and Spare~Register ($1.07\times$)---at a
hardware cost of only \textbf{1.4~KB per SM}, or 1.1\% of the
A100 L1 data cache.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/1-introduction/fig1_cache_ima_ideal.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~L1 miss rate decomposed into IMA data, IMA index, and
    non-IMA misses (stacked), alongside L2 miss rate (per-algorithm
    median, symmetric graphs).
    (b)~Ideal L1D speedup (geometric mean per algorithm; overall
    2.04$\times$ across 25 configurations).}
  \label{fig:cache-ima}
\end{figure}

% ¶1: IMA definition + universality
Graph analytics (e.g., social networks, road networks, web graphs),
sparse linear algebra, and data-intensive applications increasingly
rely on general-purpose graphics processing units (GPGPUs, called
GPUs in the rest of this paper) for
acceleration~\cite{wang2016gunrock, xu2019gardenia,
yang2022graphblast, chen2020pangolin}.
A defining characteristic of these workloads is the \emph{Indirect
Memory Access} (IMA) pattern $A[B[i]]$, in which one load's address
depends on the return value of a prior load~\cite{yu2015imp,
fu2024dmp}.
IMA fundamentally breaks spatial and temporal locality: the data
array addresses are determined at runtime and scatter unpredictably
across memory space ~\cite{talati2021prodigy, xue2024tyche}.

% ¶2: IMA breaks GPU latency hiding + Prefetching opportunity + Fig 1
NVIDIA GPUs hide memory latency through warp-level parallelism: each
Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) interleaves up to 64 concurrent warps
(groups of 32 SIMD threads sharing a single program counter),
swapping among them whenever the running warp stalls on a memory
access.
The mechanism keeps the pipeline busy as long as some warp is ready
to issue.
What breaks this hiding philosophy in IMA is the access mode itself:
each data load's address is supplied by the runtime value returned
by the preceding index load, so the two loads must execute
back-to-back as a serial dependency chain, sharply reducing the
memory-level parallelism (MLP) that warp interleaving needs to hide
latency.
The result is a pile-up of long misses---IMA instructions account
for \textbf{61--93\% of all L1 data cache misses} across six
representative graph algorithms (Figure~\ref{fig:cache-ima}, a),
and the chained index--data dependency further inflates the
effective per-IMA latency to $\approx 786$~cycles in our experiments.
Hiding latencies of this magnitude would require, by Little's Law,
roughly $196$ concurrent warps per SM---more than three times the
\textbf{64-warp} hardware ceiling---so warp-level parallelism alone
can no longer mask the stalls.

% ¶3: Prefetching as solution + ideal cache upper bound
Prefetching has long been recognized as a classical approach to
mitigating low MLP~\cite{jouppi1990stream, mowry1992software,
lee2010manythread, jog2013orchestrated}, lifting the count of
in-flight memory requests.
To quantify the ceiling on what such a prefetcher could recover, we
evaluate an ideal L1 data cache that eliminates all L1 load misses;
it achieves a geometric mean speedup of \textbf{2.04$\times$} across
25~workload configurations (Figure~\ref{fig:cache-ima}, b).

% ¶4: GPU stride prefetching — 15 years of progress, IMA blind spot
Despite this potential, the past 15~years of GPU prefetching
research has progressively advanced from inter-thread
prefetching~\cite{lee2010manythread} and scheduling--prefetch
co-design~\cite{jog2013orchestrated} to CTA-aware leading-warp
detection~\cite{koo2018caps} and variable-length stride
chains~\cite{mostofi2023snake}, consistently targeting stride and
streaming patterns~\cite{oh2016apres, oh2018wasp}.
IMA, in contrast, requires a fundamentally different prefetching mechanism:
the data load's address is determined by a runtime index value, not
by an arithmetic stride.
CAPS explicitly skips data-dependent
accesses~\cite{koo2018caps}, and Snake's chains remain
stride-based~\cite{mostofi2023snake}.

% ¶5: Spare Register — sole GPU IMA attempt
The only hardware prefetcher targeting IMA on GPUs is Spare
Register~\cite{lakshminarayana2014spare}, which detects load-pair
dependencies and stores prefetched data in idle registers, achieving
10\% average IPC improvement.
Designed and evaluated on the Fermi architecture~(2010), its
assumptions about cache hierarchy and warp scheduling no longer hold
for modern GPUs.
In the decade since, every subsequent GPU prefetcher has targeted
stride patterns exclusively~\cite{koo2018caps, oh2018wasp,
mostofi2023snake}.

% ¶6: CPU IMA prefetchers + open problem closing
On the CPU side, architects have accumulated nearly a decade of
hardware IMA prefetching, demonstrating that the problem is tractable.
IMP detects $A[B[i]]$ patterns via address
differentials~\cite{yu2015imp}, and the state-of-the-art
DMP~\cite{fu2024dmp} matches four classes of indirect patterns at
0.9\,KB.
Subsequent work has progressively addressed multi-level and
non-linear variants~\cite{cavus2020atp, kaushik2021gretch,
xue2024tyche, talati2021prodigy}.
These designs, however, all assume a single-threaded address stream
with per-core independent
state~\cite{ainsworth2019indirect}---assumptions that collapse under
the 64-warp concurrency of a GPU SM, where naive per-warp
replication would cost 57.6\,KB/SM.
GPU IMA prefetching therefore remains an open problem that demands a
prefetcher native to the GPU's execution model.

% ¶7: IMAD.WIDE — the ISA structural advantage
Rather than migrating CPU techniques, we observe that the NVIDIA
GPU ISA provides a more direct path.
When compiling an $A[B[i]]$-style IMA chain, the compiler almost
always emits the SASS instruction
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE\;Rd, Rindex, Rscale, c[base]} for the index-to-data
address computation, and this instruction encodes \emph{all} the
parameters needed to prefetch the data load:
the \emph{base address} of the data array (a kernel-lifetime constant
in constant memory), the \emph{scale factor} (element size, a
compile-time constant), and the \emph{index dependency} (the source
register linking to the preceding index load).
A single observation of this instruction therefore suffices to
extract every prefetch parameter directly from its encoding, at
extremely low cost.
The structural guarantee comes from a hardware fact: GPU pointers
are 64-bit while graph indices use 32-bit data, so computing a data
address from an index requires a 32$\times$32$+$64$\to$64
multiply--add operation that maps uniquely to \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} in
the SASS ISA, making it the compiler's obligatory choice.
Across the 36 (algorithm, GPU generation) pairs spanning our six
graph algorithms and six GPU generations (Volta through Hopper),
\textbf{34} exhibit $\geq$86\% \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} conformance,
confirming the pattern's cross-architecture stability.

% ¶8: GRASP overview + selected results
Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{GRASP} (\textbf{G}PU
\textbf{R}egister-chain \textbf{A}ware \textbf{S}ector
\textbf{P}refetcher), a hardware prefetcher that detects
\texttt{LDG} $\to$ \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} $\to$ \texttt{LDG} register
dependency chains at
the issue stage and prefetches through a two-step
index-then-data pipeline.
Observing \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} at the issue stage gives GRASP two
advantages.
First, \emph{detection overhead is negligible}: every prefetch
parameter is directly encoded in the instruction operands, so a
single observation identifies an entire IMA chain.
Second, \emph{storage is compact}: per-SM shared tables combined
with (base,\,scale) merging collapse up to 60+ IMA chains in SpMV
into only $\sim$2 table entries, requiring only $\sim$1.4\,KB/SM.
Evaluated on 28~workloads spanning six graph algorithms and five
datasets, GRASP achieves a geometric-mean speedup of
\textbf{1.18$\times$} (up to \textbf{2.22$\times$}) over an
unmodified A100 configuration.

% ¶8: Contributions
\smallskip\noindent
This paper makes the following contributions:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]
\item \textbf{IMA Characterization and IMAD.WIDE Discovery.}
  We present the first systematic quantification of IMA behavior on
  modern GPUs, showing that IMA accounts for 61--93\% of L1 misses
  with an ideal L1D headroom of 2.04$\times$ (geometric mean).
  We identify \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} as a structurally guaranteed ISA
  feature that encodes all IMA prefetch parameters, stable across
  six GPU generations.
\item \textbf{GRASP Design.}
  We propose the first dedicated IMA prefetcher for modern GPUs:
  a zero-inference design built on \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} detection,
  featuring an index--data two-step pipeline, (base,\,scale)
  merging, and per-SM shared tables at only $\sim$1.4\,KB/SM.
\item \textbf{Comprehensive Evaluation.}
  We evaluate GRASP on 28~workloads against three SOTA GPU
  prefetcher baselines (Snake, CAPS, Spare~Register),
  achieving a geometric-mean speedup of $1.18\times$
  (up to $2.22\times$) over an unmodified baseline.
\end{itemize}

\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:motivation}

\subsection{GPU Memory Hierarchy}
\label{sec:bg-hierarchy}

% ¶1: Strict description of Fig 2 (no specific numbers — those go to §2.3/§2.4)
Modern NVIDIA GPUs adopt a hierarchical organization
(Fig.~\ref{fig:gpu}).
At the top, an A100-class GPGPU contains 8 GPCs, each holding several
TPCs that pair Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) two at a time, for a
total of 108 SMs.
Each SM features four warp schedulers, a 256\,KB register file,
separate FP32, INT32, tensor and load--store units, and a private L1
data cache co-located with shared memory.
Misses from the L1 traverse an interconnect to the L2 cache, which is
partitioned into slices each tied to its own memory controller, and
ultimately to off-chip HBM.
GPUs hide this multi-level memory latency by interleaving instructions
from many concurrent warps on every SM.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/2-Background_Motivation/GPU.pdf}
  \caption{Hierarchical organization of an A100-class GPU.}
  \label{fig:gpu}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The Indirect Memory Access Pattern}
\label{sec:bg-ima}

% ¶1: CSR forces IMA — concept layer (no SASS yet)
Indirect memory access (IMA) is not an artifact of unoptimized code; it
is the natural consequence of how graphs are stored.
The Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format encodes an
$M{\times}N$ sparse matrix with three arrays
(Fig.~\ref{fig:csr}\,(a-b)):
\texttt{row\_off[i]} marks the starting offset of row~$i$,
\texttt{A\_col[j]} stores the column indices of all non-zeros in
row-major order, and
\texttt{A\_val[j]} stores the corresponding values.
Sparse matrix--vector multiplication (SpMV)---the simplest CSR
operation---computes
$y_i = \sum_{j} A_{ij}\,x_j$
by iterating \texttt{j} over each row's non-zeros and accumulating
\texttt{A\_val[j] * x[A\_col[j]]} (Fig.~\ref{fig:csr}\,(c)).
The expression \texttt{x[A\_col[j]]} is structurally an
\texttt{A[B[j]]} indirect access:
the column index drawn from \texttt{A\_col[j]} is unknown until that
load returns, after which it must be used to address the dense
element \texttt{x[A\_col[j]]}.
The same skeleton appears in BFS, SSSP, BC, CC and PageRank under the
name \emph{neighbor traversal}; SpMV is the simplest concrete instance
and serves as our running example throughout the paper.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/2-Background_Motivation/csr_spmv.pdf}
  \caption{(a-b)~SpMV CSR encoding of a $4{\times}8$ sparse matrix.
    (c)~Kernel; \texttt{x[A\_col[j]]} is the IMA chain.
    (d)~Runtime: a stride-1 index load drives a scattered data
    load.}
  \label{fig:csr}
\end{figure}

% ¶2: Conceptual three-step hardware execution (no SASS code yet)
At the hardware level, evaluating one such IMA access requires three
strictly ordered steps:
(i)~a load of the index value~\texttt{A\_col[j]} into a register;
(ii)~an arithmetic combination of that loaded value with the data
array's base pointer and a per-element scale factor to compute the
data-load address; and
(iii)~a second load that fetches the dense element from the computed
address.
Two memory loads must execute serially for every IMA access, and as
we now show, this serial dependency is what dismantles the GPU's
warp-parallel latency-hiding mechanism.

\subsection{IMA Breaks Warp Latency Hiding}
\label{sec:bg-latency}

% ¶1: Little's Law + regular-workload baseline
GPUs absorb memory latency by issuing instructions from many
concurrent warps. By Little's Law, fully hiding an effective memory
latency $L_{\mathrm{eff}}$ on one SM requires
\begin{equation}
N_{\mathrm{warp}} \,\cdot\, C \;\geq\; L_{\mathrm{eff}},
\label{eq:little}
\end{equation}
where $C$ is the average inter-issue interval per warp.
For regular workloads, $C$ is large and $L_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is small
($\approx{}50$~cycles), so a few dozen warps suffice.

% ¶2: IMA inflates both terms + Fig 4 reading (merged ¶2+¶3)
IMA breaks both terms at once. The data load cannot be issued
until the index load returns, so the per-access latency is the
sum of two serial loads:
$L_{\mathrm{chain}}=L_{\mathrm{idx}}+L_{\mathrm{data}}\approx{}786$~cycles
on our A100 simulator (487--933~cycles across individually measured
chains). Meanwhile IMA inner loops compress to only 3--5 SASS
instructions between consecutive chains, so $C$ shrinks to
3--5~cycles. Substituting into Eq.~\ref{eq:little} for each
Gardenia algorithm (Fig.~\ref{fig:warp-gap}), every workload
requires between 157 and 262 concurrent warps per SM---$2.5$ to
$4.1{\times}$ the A100's 64-warp
ceiling~\cite{nvidia2020a100}. GPU latency hiding is not
under-provisioned; it is structurally defeated.

\begin{figure}[b]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/2-Background_Motivation/warp_gap.pdf}
  \caption{Required warps per SM ($N_{\mathrm{req}}{=}L_{\mathrm{chain}}/C$)
    for each Gardenia algorithm. All workloads exceed the A100
    64-warp ceiling by $2.5${--}$4.1{\times}$.}
  \label{fig:warp-gap}
\end{figure}

% ¶3: Fig 1 phenomenology + L1-targeted prefetching opportunity (merged ¶4+¶5)
Yet the data is not far away. Returning to
Fig.~\ref{fig:cache-ima}, L1 miss rates reach 38--59\% with IMA
accounting for 61--93\% of those misses, while L2 miss rates remain
low at 11--30\%: the bytes the data load needs already reside in
on-chip L2, only L1 has missed them. A prefetcher that stages IMA data from L2 into L1
therefore has a budget of $\approx{}200$~cycles per
request---vs.~500-plus for an L2$\to$DRAM round trip---and a
ceiling of $2.0{\times}$ geomean speedup
(\S\ref{sec:intro}). An L1-targeted IMA prefetcher is the natural
remedy, if it can be built for IMA on a GPU.

\subsection{Why Existing Prefetchers Fall Short}
\label{sec:bg-prior}

% ¶1: Two threads exist; CPU detection collapses on GPU (merged ¶1+¶2)
Two research threads exist. GPU prefetchers from
\textsc{ManyThread}~\cite{lee2010manythread} through
\textsc{CAPS}~\cite{koo2018caps} and
\textsc{Snake}~\cite{mostofi2023snake} target stride patterns and
explicitly skip data-dependent loads. CPU IMA prefetchers
(IMP~\cite{yu2015imp}, DMP~\cite{fu2024dmp},
Tyche~\cite{xue2024tyche}) do handle the pattern, but their
detection mechanisms all assume a single sequential instruction
stream from one execution context. On a GPU SM, four warp
schedulers interleave instructions from many concurrent warps:
``the next index load at PC~$p$'' is drawn from a different
vertex by a different warp, and the address differential between
consecutive loads at the same PC carries no spatial meaning. The
per-core inference machinery these schemes rely on dissolves in
the multiplexed GPU stream.

% ¶2: Storage explosion — Table 1 (tightened)
Restoring detectability by replicating the per-context state
across all warps costs 36.5--57.6\,KB per SM
(Table~\ref{tab:cpu-cost})---$19$--$30\%$ of A100's 192\,KB
unified L1 budget~\cite{nvidia2020a100}. Even the smallest of the
three consumes nearly a fifth of the very cache it is meant to
assist.

\begin{table}[!b]
  \caption{Per-SM storage cost of replicating CPU IMA prefetcher
    state across the 64 warps of an A100 SM.}
  \label{tab:cpu-cost}
  \centering
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{lcccc}
    \toprule
    Prefetcher & Venue    & Per-core & Per-SM ($\times 64$) & \% of L1 \\
    \midrule
    IMP~\cite{yu2015imp}      & MICRO'15 & 0.70\,KB & 44.8\,KB & 23\% \\
    DMP~\cite{fu2024dmp}      & HPCA'24  & 0.90\,KB & 57.6\,KB & 30\% \\
    Tyche~\cite{xue2024tyche} & TACO'24  & 0.57\,KB & 36.5\,KB & 19\% \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

% ¶3: Spare Register + bridge to §2.5 (merged ¶4+¶5)
The only published GPU IMA prefetcher is Spare
Register~\cite{lakshminarayana2014spare}, which stores prefetched
data in unused registers to avoid polluting Fermi's 16\,KB L1. A
modern A100 SM has grown that L1 to 192\,KB at 32\,B sector
granularity, erasing the ``L1 too small to cache prefetches''
premise that motivated the design. In the decade since, no GPU
hardware prefetcher has revisited IMA as its primary target;
migrating CPU schemes is blocked by the multi-warp interleaving
above, and no existing approach has examined the source of IMA
information already inside the GPU itself---its SASS ISA.

\subsection{The IMAD.WIDE Insight}
\label{sec:bg-imad}

% ¶1: Key observation — IMAD.WIDE is the compiler-stable hardware signature
The runtime three-step procedure described in
\S\ref{sec:bg-ima}---index load, address arithmetic, data load---is
realized in NVIDIA SASS as a fixed three-instruction sequence:
\texttt{LDG} $\to$ \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} $\to$ \texttt{LDG}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:imad-chain}).
The middle instruction is not arbitrary.
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} is the only SASS instruction that performs a
single-cycle 32$\times$32$+$64$\to$64-bit fused multiply--add,
fusing a 32-bit index, a 32-bit element scale and a 64-bit base
address into a 64-bit pointer in one operation.
A three-instruction software replacement using \texttt{SHF},
\texttt{IADD3} and a separate move would be both slower and longer,
so nvcc has no incentive to choose it.
Fig.~\ref{fig:chain-stability} confirms this empirically:
across the six Gardenia graph algorithms compiled for six GPU
generations from Volta to Hopper, five of six exhibit
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} chain conformance $\geq{}86\%$ (BFS, SSSP, CC,
SpMV and VC), with only BC dipping to 78\% on SM70 and SM80, where
the compiler occasionally substitutes a longer LEA/IADD3 path.
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} is, in effect, the compiler-stable hardware
signature of CSR-driven IMA across the entire current generation
of NVIDIA GPUs.

% ¶2: Fig 5 reading
Fig.~\ref{fig:imad-chain} shows the chain emitted for SpMV.
The first \texttt{LDG} loads the column index into register
\texttt{R10}.
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} consumes \texttt{R10} as one of its source
operands and produces the data-load address in \texttt{R12},
which the second \texttt{LDG} then dereferences to fetch
\texttt{x[A\_col[j]]}.
What makes \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} unique is its operand structure:
the instruction explicitly carries the destination address
register (\texttt{R12}), the index source register
(\texttt{R10}), the element scale as an immediate
(\texttt{0x8}), and the base pointer of the data array as a
constant-memory reference
(\texttt{c[\,0x0\,][\,0x178\,]}, a kernel-lifetime parameter).

\begin{figure}[h]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/2-Background_Motivation/IMA_chain.pdf}
  \caption{SASS chain for \texttt{x[A\_col[j]]}. \texttt{IMAD.WIDE}
    encodes the destination register, scale (\texttt{0x8}), and
    base pointer (\texttt{c[\,0x0\,][\,0x178\,]}) as operands;
    only the index (\texttt{R10}) is dynamic.}
  \label{fig:imad-chain}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!b]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/2-Background_Motivation/chain_stability.pdf}
  \caption{\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} chain conformance for the six
    Gardenia algorithms across NVIDIA SM generations
    (SM70~Volta--SM90~Hopper).}
  \label{fig:chain-stability}
\end{figure}

% ¶3: Why this matters — zero-inference detection
This operand structure is the core of the GRASP design.
A hardware unit that observes a single \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} at the
issue stage can extract the scale and the base directly from the
instruction encoding, identify the source register that produced
the index, and deduce the upcoming data-load address as soon as
the dependent index value returns from L1/L2.
No address-stream snooping, no per-warp differential history, and
no PC-level shift inference are required.
The detection problem reduces from runtime statistical inference
to a single-instruction observation, and the per-warp state
explosion that would have made CPU prefetcher migration prohibitive
(\S\ref{sec:bg-prior}) does not arise:
a single shared table can serve all 64 warps on an SM, because
every warp executes the same \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} instruction at the
same PC.

% ¶4: Bridge to §3 (now Design — Key Insight section is removed)
This is the structural opening that the rest of the paper exploits.
The next section presents GRASP, a hardware prefetcher built around
this single observation.



%%% ====================================================================
%%% §3 GRASP Design
%%% ====================================================================
\section{GRASP Design}
\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Overview}
\label{sec:design-overview}

GRASP realizes the \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} observation of
\S\ref{sec:bg-imad} as a per-SM hardware prefetcher operating at
the instruction issue stage.
It detects IMA chains via the
\texttt{LDG}\,$\to$\,\texttt{IMAD.WIDE}\,$\to$\,\texttt{LDG}
register dependency, then issues a two-step prefetch---index
first, then data---using a per-PC iteration stride.
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the hardware components in their per-SM
context, and Fig.~\ref{fig:flow} traces the algorithmic flow from
chain detection through demand-load hit.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/3-Design/Top-Level_Architecture_Diagram.pdf}
  \caption{GRASP per-SM hardware overview (training path solid, prefetch path dashed).}
  \label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

The training path (solid arrows in Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}) follows
issued instructions of two \emph{tracked warps} through the CD,
where register-dependency matching populates the CT and TT.
The prefetch path (dashed arrows) is triggered on every demand
load that hits a CT entry with a converged stride: the Index
Prefetch Unit (IPU) issues a prefetch for the next iteration's
index, the Prefetch Request Buffer (PRB) tracks it across the L2
round trip, and the Data Prefetch Unit (DPU) computes and issues
the corresponding data prefetch when the index value returns.
All components are per-SM shared rather than per-warp replicated:
because every warp executes the same \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} at the
same PC, a single shared table serves all 64 warps.
We now describe each step, starting with how the chain detector
identifies the dependency at issue.

\begin{figure}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/3-Design/Flowchart.pdf}
  \caption{GRASP algorithmic flow: detect, register, learn, prefetch, fill, hit.}
  \label{fig:flow}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Detecting Chains at Issue}
\label{sec:design-cd}

The Chain Detector must identify the
\texttt{LDG}\,$\to$\,\texttt{IMAD.WIDE}\,$\to$\,\texttt{LDG}
sequence at issue, before either load completes, so the index
prefetch for the next iteration can be launched one iteration
ahead. Per-warp register tracking across 64 warps and heavy
multi-warp interleaving would explode the state budget; we avoid
both by exploiting two properties of \texttt{IMAD.WIDE}. First,
it carries the array base and element scale directly as
instruction operands, so the key fields can be read by inspection
rather than inferred from address history (\S\ref{sec:bg-imad}).
Second, every warp executes the same chain PCs, so sampling two
\emph{tracked warps} is enough to discover every chain.

Detection thus reduces to a three-step FIFO match
(Fig.~\ref{fig:cd}): a tracked-warp \texttt{LDG} pushes
\texttt{(PC, dest\_reg)} onto the 20-entry shared FIFO; an
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} whose source matches a FIFO entry records the
index PC, base, scale, and IMAD destination register; and a
subsequent \texttt{LDG} reading that destination confirms the
chain and writes it to the CT and TT. A FIFO entry is invalidated
when its destination is overwritten or consumed by a non-IMAD
instruction, so no spurious chains survive.

\begin{figure}[!b]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/3-Design/Chain_detect.pdf}
  \caption{Chain detection: tracked-warp instructions feed a shared FIFO whose three-step match confirms an IMA chain.}
  \label{fig:cd}
\end{figure}

We size the CD FIFO at 20 entries (SpMV's $\times16$ unroll peaks
at 17) and track two warps per SM; the sensitivity to both is in
\S\ref{sec:eval}.

\subsection{Storing Chains Compactly}
\label{sec:design-tables}

The Chain Table (CT) and Target Table (TT) jointly store every
detected chain in tens of bytes apiece. The challenge is loop
unrolling: SpMV's $\times16$ Duff's device produces 30+ distinct
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} PCs that all share the same
\texttt{(base, scale)}, so a naive PC-keyed table would need
hundreds of entries. We exploit the fact that unrolling preserves
the constant operands, making \texttt{(base, scale)} a natural
merge key. The CT dispatches each unique index PC to an entry
that holds its stride state, while the TT coalesces all chains
sharing the same \texttt{(base, scale)} into one entry; multiple
CT entries point to the same TT entry through a
\texttt{tt\_idx[]} field (Fig.~\ref{fig:tables}). PC merging thus
happens at the TT rather than the CT.

Each CT entry carries the index PC tag, up to three TT indices
(supporting BC's reverse pass where one index feeds three arrays),
and LRU bits; entries are flushed on kernel switch to avoid stale
stride state. Each TT entry is a 5\,B slot holding only a 32-bit
base tag and 3-bit scale. Fig.~\ref{fig:tables} illustrates the
merge for SpMV: three PCs all reference
\texttt{c[0x0][0x178]} with scale~4, their CT entries set
\texttt{tt\_idx[0]\,=\,0}, and one TT entry \texttt{(x\_base, 4)}
services them all.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/3-Design/CT_TT.pdf}
  \caption{CT/TT structure: SpMV's unrolled \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} PCs collapse onto one TT entry via the shared \texttt{(base, scale)} key.}
  \label{fig:tables}
\end{figure}

Each CT entry also holds a per-PC stride state, updated by the
tracked warp's demand loads; two consecutive agreeing
observations freeze the stride. Stride state is reset on warp
exit to prevent a CTA's tail from contaminating the next CTA's
first iteration (raising the per-chain hit rate from 29\% to
60\%). An optional \emph{speculative stride hint} lets a compiler
bypass the observation phase by passing the element size directly,
which helps kernels whose stride converges slowly. We size the CT
at 32 entries and the TT at 8, with a confidence threshold of
two; the sensitivity curve in \S\ref{sec:eval} shows these values
sit well past the knee.

\subsection{The Two-Step Prefetch}
\label{sec:design-pipeline}

The Index Prefetch Unit (IPU), Prefetch Request Buffer (PRB), and
Data Prefetch Unit (DPU) turn CT/TT lookups into actual L1 fills.
Their joint design is the central novelty of GRASP. The challenge
is that the data address depends on the \emph{value} returned by
the index load, so it cannot be prefetched until that value
arrives; CPU solutions based on per-thread lookahead PCs would
replicate the prefetch state 64 times on a GPU SM, while prior
GPU prefetchers (Snake, CAPS) sidestep the issue by predicting
only the index stride. We instead split the prefetch into two
pipelined stages: an index prefetch based on the learned stride,
followed on its fill by a dependent data prefetch computed from
\texttt{(base, scale)}. The PRB carries the chain metadata across
the round trip.

When a demand load hits a CT entry with a valid stride, the IPU
issues an index prefetch for
$\text{addr}\,+\,\text{stride}\,\times\,\text{distance}$ and
allocates a PRB entry holding only the CT index ($\sim$1\,B).
The L1 controller routes the fill through the PRB, where the DPU
reads the returned index value and computes
\begin{equation}
  \text{data\_addr} = \text{base} + \text{index\_value} \times
  \text{scale},
  \label{eq:data-addr}
\end{equation}
emitting one data prefetch per target in the CT entry's
\texttt{tt\_idx[]}. Sector-level tracking lets multi-sector index
fills drain independently before the PRB entry is released.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/3-Design/prefetch_pipe.pdf}
  \caption{Two-step prefetch pipeline overlapping both L2 round trips with the prior demand-load latency.}
  \label{fig:pipe}
\end{figure}

Fig.~\ref{fig:pipe} makes the resulting overlap concrete.
On the demand-only path, a single IMA chain pays roughly
${\sim}560$ cycles for the index round trip and another
${\sim}560$ cycles for the dependent data round trip---about
$1{,}120$ cycles of fully serialized memory latency that the
warp scheduler cannot hide.
GRASP issues the index prefetch one iteration ahead, so its
${\sim}560$-cycle round trip overlaps the prior iteration's
demand load; the dependent data prefetch then chains directly
off the index fill rather than waiting on a second demand.
Both L2 round trips collapse into the inter-iteration interval,
and the next demand index and data loads find their lines
already in L1.

The default prefetch \emph{distance} is one---unusual for a
prefetcher, but imposed by SIMT: active lane counts can drop
sharply between iterations (e.g., 32\,$\to$\,4 under worklist
compaction), and a larger distance pre-allocates prefetches
against the current mask, wasting 24--28 requests per mask
transition at distance~4 versus at most ten at distance~1. The
PRB holds 512 entries, oversized to absorb bursts.

\subsection{Adaptive Throttling}
\label{sec:design-tc}

The Throttle Controller prevents prefetch-induced pollution under
MSHR pressure without stalling useful prefetches in benign
phases. A static MSHR threshold either over- or under-throttles,
and prefetch quality is non-stationary: BFS stays above 90\%
accuracy while SpMV alternates between clean and polluted phases
that demand a tighter gate. We therefore let the MSHR threshold
track \emph{recent} accuracy via a sliding-window controller
(Fig.~\ref{fig:tc}).

A 5\,000-cycle window measures \texttt{pf\_useful}/\texttt{pf\_useless}
and the effective threshold is linearly interpolated between
\texttt{mshr\_lo}\,=\,50\% (at accuracy~$\le$~30\%) and
\texttt{mshr\_hi}\,=\,90\% (at accuracy~$\ge$~60\%). Crossing the
threshold triggers a 200-cycle cooldown that suppresses data
prefetches; index prefetches are exempt, since dropping them
would break the two-step pipeline of the next iteration.

\begin{figure}[b!]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/3-Design/throttle.drawio.pdf}
  \caption{Adaptive throttle: the MSHR threshold tracks sliding-window prefetch accuracy, opening cooldown windows that suppress data prefetches.}
  \label{fig:tc}
\end{figure}

This feedback loop is what separates the simpler T40C200
static-threshold variant we evaluate as a baseline from the
adaptive D5b version that delivers consistent gains across the 24
workload$\,\times\,$dataset combinations in \S\ref{sec:eval}.

\paragraph{Hardware budget.}
GRASP's per-SM storage footprint---CD FIFOs, CT, TT, PRB, IST, and
throttle counters combined---totals approximately 1.4\,KB, with the
detailed breakdown and comparison against prior GPU and CPU
prefetchers deferred to \S\ref{sec:eval}.

\input{table_templates}  % Loads tab:grasp-budget for §5.5, tab:algorithms
% and tab:datasets for §4, and tab:performance for §5.


%%% ====================================================================
%%% §4 Methodology
%%% ====================================================================
\section{Experimental Methodology}
\label{sec:method}

\noindent\textbf{Simulation.}\hspace{0.5em}
We evaluate GRASP using Accel-Sim v1.3.0~\cite{khairy2020accelsim}
on top of GPGPU-Sim 4.2.0, configured to model the NVIDIA A100
(SM80) GPU. Table~\ref{tab:gpu-config} lists the full simulator
and GPU parameters. Each application is simulated until all
kernels complete, and per-kernel IPC and aggregated cache
statistics are recorded.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Benchmarks and Datasets.}\hspace{0.5em}
We evaluate on nine graph and irregular kernels drawn from three
benchmark suites (Table~\ref{tab:algorithms}): six core graph
algorithms---BFS, SSSP, BC, CC, SpMV, and VC---from the Gardenia
suite~\cite{xu2019gardenia}; one Maximal Independent Set kernel
(MIS) and one graph Coloring kernel from the Pannotia
suite~\cite{che2013pannotia}; and one Minimum Spanning Tree kernel
(MST) from LonestarGPU~\cite{burtscher2012irregular}. The Gardenia
kernels are run on five real-world graphs spanning citation, web,
social, and road networks (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}); MIS additionally
uses \texttt{flickr}, Color uses \texttt{ecology1}, and MST uses an
\texttt{RMAT-12} input. After excluding kernel/dataset combinations
that are infeasible on the simulator (e.g., VC on \texttt{flickr}
and \texttt{roadNet-CA} due to coloring overflow), the evaluation
comprises approximately 33 algorithm/dataset configurations.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Comparison Points.}\hspace{0.5em}
We compare GRASP against four baselines, referenced as (1)--(4)
throughout Section~\ref{sec:eval}.
\textbf{(1)~No~Prefetch} disables hardware prefetching entirely and
provides the performance lower bound.
\textbf{(2)~Snake}~\cite{mostofi2023snake} is the variable-length
stride-chain prefetcher representing the current GPU stride state of
the art.
\textbf{(3)~CAPS}~\cite{koo2018caps} is a CTA-aware leading-warp
stride prefetcher that explicitly excludes data-dependent loads.
\textbf{(4)~Spare~Register}~\cite{lakshminarayana2014spare} is the
only prior GPU prefetcher targeting indirect memory access; it
propagates value tags through spare registers to prefetch one level
of indirection, and we re-implement it on GPGPU-Sim~4.x for fair
comparison on the SM80 platform. The Ideal-L1D upper bound used to
quantify prefetching headroom in Section~\ref{sec:bg-latency} is not
listed as a baseline---it is not a physically realizable
prefetcher---but is shown alongside (1)--(4) in the result figures
of Section~\ref{sec:eval} as a reference ceiling.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Metrics.}\hspace{0.5em}
We report four metrics, all restricted to IMA loads identified by
the chain analysis (i.e., the denominator excludes non-IMA L1
traffic), so that the numbers isolate prefetcher behavior on the
access pattern of interest.
\textbf{IPC~Speedup} is the ratio of geometric-mean IPC under each
comparison point to that of (1)~No~Prefetch.
\textbf{IMA~Coverage} is the fraction of IMA-related demand misses
that the prefetcher converts into hits.
\textbf{Accuracy} is the fraction of issued IMA prefetches that are
eventually consumed by a matching demand request before eviction.
\textbf{Timeliness}, reported separately from accuracy, is the
fraction of useful prefetches that returned to L1 \emph{before} the
matching demand arrived; unlike prior work that conflates the two,
we report Accuracy and Timeliness as independent quantities so that
early-but-stale and on-time-but-incorrect prefetches can be
diagnosed separately. Per-SM hardware overhead is reported as part
of the cost analysis in Section~\ref{sec:eval}.


%%% ====================================================================
%%% §5 Evaluation
%%% ====================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We evaluate GRASP on 28 workloads (detailed in
\S\ref{sec:method}) against the four baselines defined there.
The evaluation begins with prefetch quality in isolation, then
explains the underlying mechanism, translates these into
end-to-end performance, and closes with sensitivity analyses
and hardware cost.


\subsection{Prefetch Quality}
\label{sec:eval-quality}

\begin{figure*}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/5-evaluation/quality.pdf}
  \caption{Prefetch quality across 27 workloads. GRASP
    averages 58\% coverage, 78\% timeliness, and 71\% accuracy---
    2--58$\times$ above the stride-only baselines. SR is
    reconstructed from IPC speedup (see text).}
  \label{fig:quality}
\end{figure*}

Fig.~\ref{fig:quality}(a) reports IMA coverage---the fraction
of IMA-tagged L1 reads each prefetcher converts into hits or
hit-reserved entries. GRASP averages 58\%, versus 18\% for
Snake, 1\% for CAPS, and 25\% for Spare~Register~(SR). Snake and
CAPS detect only regular strides and by construction exclude
data-dependent loads; SR captures one hop of indirection but
cannot share learned patterns across the 64 warps of an~SM.
GRASP's coverage exceeds 65\% on every flickr and road-network
input but falls to 37--43\% on the sparse cit-Patents SpMV, VC,
and CC kernels, whose Pattern~III/IV second hops are
intrinsically unpredictable.

Fig.~\ref{fig:quality}(b) reports timeliness---the fraction of
\emph{useful} prefetches whose data has already returned to L1
when the matching demand issues. Unlike prior work we report
coverage and timeliness as independent quantities
(\S\ref{sec:method}). GRASP averages 78\%, an order of magnitude
above CAPS (3\%) and well ahead of Snake (65\%) and SR (54\%):
the index pipeline issues the first-hop prefetch one or more
iterations ahead of the demand so that the data hop fires with
the resolved index already in L1. Timeliness drops to 25\% on
\texttt{spmv\_cit} where the sparse row chain is shorter than
the L2 round-trip.

Fig.~\ref{fig:quality}(c) reports accuracy---the fraction of
issued prefetches eventually consumed by a demand. GRASP
averages 71\%, comparable to Snake (65\%) and well above CAPS
(3\%) and SR (52\%). It exceeds 99\% on the six deterministic
kernels (BFS, SSSP, and BC on \texttt{cit\_dir} and
\texttt{road\_sym}), where the throttle admits only the most
confident prefetches, and drops to 18\% on \texttt{spmv\_cit}
and 24\% on \texttt{vc\_cit} because each outer worklist jump
invalidates the CT \texttt{iter\_stride}.
SR's instrumented quality counters were unavailable; its bars
are reconstructed from its IPC speedup and shown as a reference
envelope rather than measured ground truth.


\subsection{Mechanism Analysis}
\label{sec:eval-mech}

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/5-evaluation/mechanism.pdf}
  \caption{GRASP mechanism analysis. (a)~Per-algorithm L1 IMA
    miss reduction. (b)~Pipeline funnel of successful delivery,
    throttle drops, MSHR reservation failures, and residual
    outcomes.}
  \label{fig:mechanism}
\end{figure}

Fig.~\ref{fig:mechanism}(a) shows per-algorithm L1 IMA miss
reduction. CC and MIS lead at 31\% and 30\%, followed by BFS
(27\%) and SSSP (25\%)---kernels whose inner loops train IST
quickly. CLR (18\%), SpMV (14\%), and BC (12\%) form a middle
cluster with more diverse access patterns, and VC sits at only
4\% because its $\times 16$ loop unroll inflates the distinct
IMA PC count so that most chains never reach the training
threshold. MST is excluded: its kernel has no measurable IMA
chain on our inputs.

Fig.~\ref{fig:mechanism}(b) decomposes GRASP's prefetch pipeline
into \emph{Got Data}, \emph{Throttled}, \emph{Idx/Data RFAIL},
and \emph{Other}. CC has the healthiest pipeline (66\% Got
Data), directly explaining its 31\% miss reduction. SpMV and VC
are dominated by Throttled (42\% and 27\%) and Idx~RFAIL (28\%
and 35\%): their bandwidth-saturated inner loops push MSHR
occupancy above the throttle's high-water mark and the few
surviving attempts lose the reservation race to demand loads.
MIS reveals a third mode---53\% throttled because its short
kernel never stabilizes the sliding-window accuracy estimate, so
the throttle stays conservative. Across all eight algorithms the
miss reductions come not from brute-force issuance but from the
throttle's selectivity, which preserves L1 bandwidth for the
prefetches most likely to land on time.


\subsection{Overall Performance vs State-of-the-Art}
\label{sec:eval-perf}

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/5-evaluation/speedup_vs_sota.pdf}
  \caption{IPC speedup over No-Prefetch across 28 workloads.
    GRASP averages $1.18\times$ (up to $2.22\times$ on
    \texttt{cc\_flickr}), 11--18~pp ahead of Snake, CAPS, and
    Spare~Register. Bars exceeding $1.30\times$ are clipped and
    labelled with their true value.}
  \label{fig:speedup}
\end{figure}

Fig.~\ref{fig:speedup} shows IPC speedup over the No-Prefetch
baseline across all 28 workloads. GRASP averages
\textbf{1.18$\times$}, substantially ahead of Snake
(1.04$\times$), CAPS (1.00$\times$), and Spare~Register
(1.07$\times$). Its largest gains come on frontier-driven graph
kernels over dense inputs: 2.22$\times$ on \texttt{cc\_flickr},
1.71$\times$ on \texttt{cc\_web}, 1.56$\times$ on
\texttt{bfs\_web}, 1.47$\times$ on \texttt{sssp\_web}, and
1.37$\times$ on \texttt{spmv\_web}---workloads where IST trains
quickly (\S\ref{sec:eval-quality}) and the throttle keeps Got
Data above 50\% (\S\ref{sec:eval-mech}).

The gap over prior GPU prefetchers reflects their stride-only
designs. Snake's variable-length stride chains explicitly
exclude data-dependent loads (\S\ref{sec:related-stride}),
limiting it to below 1.10$\times$ on every graph workload; CAPS
filters out indirect addressing entirely and its GMEAN is
neutral; Spare~Register captures one hop of indirection but
tracks a single warp at a time on Fermi-era ISA and cannot share
patterns across the 64-warp~SM.

Six workloads are near-parity or regress: \texttt{cc\_cit}
($-3.7$\%), \texttt{cc\_road} ($+0.1$\%), \texttt{spmv\_cit}
($-1.8$\%), \texttt{spmv\_road} ($-1.0$\%), \texttt{vc\_cit}
($+1.9$\%), and \texttt{vc\_web} ($+1.9$\%). Three root causes
explain them. The CC cases are Pattern~IV pointer chasing: the
second-hop data address is data-dependent and issued prefetches
are dropped under MSHR contention (Fig.~\ref{fig:mechanism}(b)).
The sparse SpMV cases run on graphs of average degree $\sim$3--5
where the baseline L1 already hits on \texttt{col\_idx}, leaving
no miss headroom to recapture. VC's $\times 16$ loop unroll
spreads the IMA load across 16 distinct PCs, only 4--5 of which
reach IST's confidence threshold before the kernel ends. All
regressions stay within 4\%.


\subsection{Sensitivity and Ablation}
\label{sec:eval-sens}

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/5-evaluation/component_ablation.pdf}
  \caption{Component ablation. Data-only and Index-only
    contributions are largely additive; Full GRASP averages
    $1.22\times$ on the 20 ablation workloads.}
  \label{fig:ablation}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/5-evaluation/throttle.pdf}
  \caption{Throttle policy comparison. IPC is insensitive to
    the throttle choice (1.20$\times$ for all three), but
    coverage doubles from 23\% (Default) to 47\% (D5b).}
  \label{fig:throttle}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/5-evaluation/sensitivity.pdf}
  \caption{Sensitivity to (a)~prefetch distance $D$ and
    (b)~per-SM storage budget~$S$, normalized per algorithm
    group. $D{=}1$ is optimal for every group except CC, and
    16 of 20 workloads are flat across $S_1$--$S_4$.}
  \label{fig:sens}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Component ablation.}
We disable each half of GRASP's prefetch pipeline to isolate
their contributions. \emph{Data-only} prefetches only the
second-hop data using demand-issued index values;
\emph{Index-only} prefetches only the index and leaves the data
hop on demand; \emph{Full} is GRASP as described in
\S\ref{sec:design}. Fig.~\ref{fig:ablation} shows that Data-only
averages $1.13\times$, Index-only $1.08\times$, and Full
$1.22\times$ over the 20 workloads with ablation data. The two
halves are largely additive because they target different
traffic: the data hop is the latency-critical end of the chain,
while the index hop saturates DRAM bandwidth on the row-pointer
stream (Index-only reaches $1.22\times$ on \texttt{spmv\_wg}).
The sole exception is \texttt{cc\_rd}, where Full slightly trails
Data-only because the index pipeline adds MSHR pressure on a
sparse graph whose data hop alone was already sufficient.

\paragraph{Throttle policy.}
We compare our adaptive throttle (D5b) against no throttle
(Default) and a static MSHR-threshold variant (T40C200).
Fig.~\ref{fig:throttle}(a) shows that all three reach the same
$1.20\times$ IPC GMEAN, but Fig.~\ref{fig:throttle}(b) shows a
striking coverage gap: Default averages 23\% IMA data coverage,
while D5b and T40C200 reach 47\% and 46\% respectively. Without
a throttle, GRASP fires prefetches aggressively enough that half
are dropped on MSHR reservation failure (Fig.~\ref{fig:mechanism}(b)),
and actionable coverage is cut in half. The adaptive policy
preserves end-to-end IPC while doubling the useful work
extracted from the prefetch queue---headroom that a future
design can exploit with tighter MSHR management.

\paragraph{Distance and storage sensitivity.}
Fig.~\ref{fig:sens}(a) sweeps the prefetch distance
$D\in\{1,2,4,8\}$ and (b) the per-SM storage budget
$S\in\{S_1{=}712\,\text{B},\,S_4{=}3.6\,\text{KB}\}$.
For most algorithm groups $D{=}1$ is optimal: larger distances
degrade BFS, SSSP, BC, and SpMV by 2--5\% through cache
pollution. The exception is CC, which gains 11\% at $D{=}8$:
its worklist has large batch distances between iterations, so
an aggressive lookahead prefetches the next frontier's indices
before they are needed. Storage sensitivity is negligible---16
of 20 workloads are completely flat across $S_1$--$S_4$, and
only SpMV and VC show variations under 3~pp. GRASP's 712\,B
default already sits at the knee of both curves, so we fix
$D{=}1$ and $S{=}S_1$ for all reported results.


\subsection{Hardware Cost}
\label{sec:eval-cost}

\begin{table}[!htbp]
  \caption{GRASP per-SM storage budget (default configuration).
    Stride state and confidence counter are embedded in each CT
    entry; the throttle controller's sliding-window state is a
    fixed scalar.}
  \label{tab:grasp-budget}
  \centering
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lcrr@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Component} & \textbf{Entries} & \textbf{Per-Entry} & \textbf{Total} \\
    \midrule
    CT (Chain Table)          & 32  & ${\sim}17$\,B & 544\,B \\
    TT (Target Table)         & 8   & ${\sim}5$\,B  & 40\,B  \\
    PRB (Prefetch Req. Buffer)& 512 & ${\sim}1$\,B  & 512\,B \\
    CD FIFO                   & 20  & ${\sim}15$\,B & 300\,B \\
    SM global state           & 1   & ${\sim}2$\,B  & 2\,B   \\
    TC sliding window         & ---           & ---  & ${\sim}20$\,B  \\
    \midrule
    \textbf{Total}            &     &               & \textbf{${\sim}1.4$\,KB} \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:grasp-budget} lists GRASP's per-SM storage
breakdown. The total of 1.4\,KB is dominated by the Chain Table
(544\,B) and the Prefetch Request Buffer (512\,B); CD FIFOs, TT,
and throttle state account for the remaining 362\,B. Per-warp
this works out to roughly 22\,B---an order of magnitude smaller
than a single thread's register-file slice.

As a fraction of A100's 128\,KB L1D, GRASP adds only 1.1\%.
Compared to CPU IMA prefetchers (IMP 0.7\,KB/core,
DMP 0.9\,KB/core, Tyche 0.57\,KB/core), GRASP fits in the same
envelope. Crucially, the 1.4\,KB is shared by all 64 warps on
the SM, so the effective per-warp cost of 22\,B is roughly
one-third of the per-thread CPU overhead.

Against prior GPU prefetchers, GRASP matches Spare~Register's
${\sim}1.4$\,KB per-SM envelope but delivers $1.18\times$
GMEAN speedup versus SR's $1.07\times$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:speedup}).
Against Snake's ${\sim}0.8$\,KB, GRASP's additional 0.6\,KB
buys coverage of Patterns~I--III which the stride-only Snake
cannot reach (\S\ref{sec:eval-quality}).


%%% ====================================================================
%%% §6 Related Work
%%% ====================================================================
\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

GRASP is the first dedicated IMA prefetcher for modern GPU
architectures, and the first to exploit ISA-exposed structural
information for zero-inference chain detection. We position it
against four lines of prior work.

\subsection{CPU IMA Prefetchers}
\label{sec:related-cpu}

CPU hardware prefetchers have explored multiple strategies for
detecting indirect access patterns at runtime.
IMP~\cite{yu2015imp} pioneered address-difference matching with
shift-search, inferring the relation between index and data streams
by accumulating address sequences that GRASP sidesteps through
direct ISA extraction.
Prodigy~\cite{talati2021prodigy} encodes a data-indirection graph at
compile time and feeds it to a runtime prefetcher, requiring
compiler co-design that GRASP avoids.
DMP~\cite{fu2024dmp}, the current CPU SOTA, uses differential-sequence
matching to identify single, range, multi-level, and multi-way
indirection pairs, yet still operates on a black-box address stream.
DVR~\cite{naithani2023dvr} introduces a decoupled vector-runahead
subthread that speculatively vectorizes indirect chains on
out-of-order cores, a microarchitectural resource unavailable under
SIMT execution.
Tyche~\cite{xue2024tyche} propagates dependencies bilaterally through
short register chains, a mechanism that is infeasible to replicate
under the 64-warp SIMT context of a modern GPU SM.
Additional CPU-side IMA prefetchers explore temporal, differential,
runahead, and slice-based
detection~\cite{cavus2020atp,kaushik2021gretch,ainsworth2018event,naithani2021vectorrunahead,naithani2020precise,litz2022crisp,bakhshalipour2018domino,fu2025magellan}.
All of these mechanisms assume a single-threaded instruction stream
with per-core state; directly replicating them per GPU warp would
incur the per-SM storage cost analyzed in
Section~\ref{sec:bg-prior}.

\subsection{GPU Prefetchers}
\label{sec:related-stride}

GPU prefetching research has steadily advanced from fixed strides to
chains of strides, yet every proposal in this line assumes memory
addresses can be predicted without consulting intermediate loaded
values.
MT-Prefetch~\cite{lee2010manythread} introduced many-thread-aware
stride detection with warp-ID indexing, establishing the stride-only
baseline for a decade of follow-on work.
CAPS~\cite{koo2018caps} added cooperative-thread-array-aware stride
detection while explicitly skipping data-dependent loads---the exact
class that GRASP targets.
APRES~\cite{oh2016apres} classifies loads by access characteristics
before prefetching, but its classifier recognises only regular
strides.
Snake~\cite{mostofi2023snake} introduces variable-length chains of
strides with decoupling and throttling, sharing the structural
vocabulary of ``chains'' with GRASP; the decisive difference is that
Snake's chain elements are constant strides, whereas GRASP's chains
carry data-value dependencies expressed directly by IMAD.WIDE
operands.
Further GPU prefetcher proposals explore orchestrated scheduling,
warp-progress monitoring, stream patterns, energy-aware triggering,
programmable shader-based prefetching, and unified-memory-aware
prefetching~\cite{jog2013orchestrated,oh2018wasp,neves2018stream,sethia2013apogee,woo2010compass,ganguly2019interplay,guo2018dsap,panda2017gmap}.
The sole prior GPU prefetcher to address indirect access directly is
Spare Register~\cite{lakshminarayana2014spare}, which propagates
value tags through spare registers to fetch one indirection level on
the Fermi (2010) architecture; its three-iteration training latency
and one-to-one index-to-data mapping have not been revisited in the
intervening decade.

\subsection{Adjacent Directions}
\label{sec:related-adjacent}

Three adjacent lines target the same memory-wall symptom along
different axes. Software prefetching on GPUs and CPUs inserts
explicit prefetch instructions through compiler
analysis~\cite{jain2013linearize,ainsworth2019indirect,jain2024dlrm,deng2024swprefetch,sotiropoulos2025asap},
trading kernel-size inflation and workload-specific tuning for
latency hiding that GRASP delivers without recompilation.
Specialised GPU prefetchers tackle disjoint subsystems---ray-tracing
BVH traversal~\cite{chou2023treelet}, TLB-fill
latency~\cite{ha2025latpc}, and warp-scheduling
coupling~\cite{posluns2025tsp}---and are composable with GRASP.
Hardware accelerators for graph and irregular
workloads~\cite{ham2016graphicionado,mukkara2018hats,ahn2015tesseract,rahman2020graphpulse,geng2021igcn,orenes2022maple}
replace the GPU pipeline with custom dataflows, an axis orthogonal
to GRASP's cache-layer enhancement.
GRASP thus occupies the previously empty cell at the intersection of
\textit{GPU}, \textit{hardware-only}, and \textit{IMA-aware}.


%%% ====================================================================
%%% §7 Conclusion
%%% ====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Indirect memory access dominates L1 misses in GPU graph
analytics and sparse workloads, yet fifteen years of GPU
prefetching has targeted only stride patterns. We showed that
NVIDIA's SASS instruction \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} already encodes
every parameter a data-load prefetcher needs---base pointer,
element scale, and index source register---turning chain
detection from runtime statistical inference into a
single-instruction observation at the issue stage. Building on
this, GRASP detects
\texttt{LDG}$\to$\texttt{IMAD.WIDE}$\to$\texttt{LDG} chains and
runs a two-step index-then-data prefetch pipeline from a per-SM
shared \emph{(base, scale)}-keyed table. On 28 A100 graph
workloads, GRASP delivers a geometric-mean speedup of
$1.18\times$ (up to $2.22\times$) at only $1.4$\,KB per SM,
outperforming Snake, CAPS, and Spare~Register and showing that
ISA-exposed structural information can replace statistical
inference in hardware prefetcher design.
